Getting started: installing Python and Jupyter on Windows

Before analysing research data, you need a working place to write and run Python. This chapter guides you through installing Python, setting up Jupyter Notebook and checking that the computer can find the correct Python installation. Think of it as preparing your laboratory bench before starting an experiment.

Watch simulation: preview the complete Windows setup, project environment, JupyterLab launch and troubleshooting walkthrough. It is a labelled teaching animation; it does not install software or change your computer.

Download the current stable 64-bit Python 3 installer from python.org/downloads (choose a release your packages support, such as 3.11 or 3.12). Run it, tick Add python.exe to PATH, choose Install Now (current user) and finish. Verify in Command Prompt. If anything fails, use the troubleshooting cells. This chapter is for understanding and reproducing the setup; you do not need to repeat it.

Teaching and advanced learning clues
  • Demonstrate the three version commands live and ask learners to explain each output.
  • Seed a PATH fault in a practice laptop and let pairs diagnose it.
  • Have learners write their own install checklist.
  • Create a venv per project and compare pip freeze output between two.
  • Read pip check output and resolve one conflict.
  • Script the folder setup in a .bat file.
Check Python, py and pipTERMINAL
python uses whichever Python is first on PATH; py is the Windows launcher that can pick a version; python -m pip runs the pip that belongs to that exact Python. Dependencies: Terminal (Command Prompt or PowerShell). Common error: wrong file path, column name or package not installed in this kernel.
python --version
py --version
python -m pip --version
Output depends on your own computer.
Run after: No prior chapter; run these commands in Windows Terminal.
If it fails: Command not recognised: confirm Python/Jupyter is installed and PATH is refreshed. Permission error: use a folder you own; do not change execution policy without checking device policy.
PATH troubleshootingTERMINAL
If python is not recognised, rerun the installer ticking Add to PATH, or add the Python and Scripts folders in Environment Variables. where shows which executable runs. Dependencies: Terminal (Command Prompt or PowerShell). Common error: wrong file path, column name or package not installed in this kernel. Use where.exe in PowerShell; where alone is a PowerShell alias and may not show executable paths.
where.exe python
where.exe py
py -0p
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"

Chapter 1: Preliminaries — Python, Jupyter and your research environment

This chapter explains where Python code runs and how notebooks, cells, kernels and packages fit together. You will learn how to run code in the right order, inspect results and manage the tools that add scientific functions to Python.

Python is the language; Jupyter Notebook is a browser interface running Python code in a kernel; packages add features; virtual environments isolate package versions. JupyterLab is the newer interface; Anaconda is a distribution bundling Python, packages and conda.

Teaching and advanced learning clues
  • Teach cell order by deliberately running cells out of order.
  • Ask learners to predict a cell's output before running it.
  • Show Restart and Run All early.
  • Use Restart and Run All as your final test before saving.
  • Learn Markdown headings to document every decision.
  • Explore the Jupyter command palette.
FIRST NOTEBOOK CELLNOTEBOOK CELL
Run once at the top of a notebook. Checks versions and sets display options. Windows-specific setup is explained separately; the analysis code is not restricted to Windows.
import sys, platform
if platform.system() != 'Windows':
    print(
        'The installation instructions target Windows; '
        'the Python analysis examples are portable.'
    )
assert platform.architecture()[0] == '64bit', 'Install 64-bit Python'
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, scipy, statsmodels
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
import scipy.stats as st
import statsmodels.api as sm, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
np.random.seed(2026)
pd.set_option('display.max_columns',50)
print(sys.version)
print(platform.system(), platform.release(), platform.architecture()[0])
for m in (np,pd,scipy,statsmodels): print(m.__name__, m.__version__)
Output depends on your own computer.
Run after: Chapter 0 setup; select the Biomedical kernel after installing packages.

Choose the right scientific Python libraryNOTEBOOK CELL
The book introduces NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, IPython/Jupyter, SciPy, scikit-learn and statsmodels. Each has a different role; use the simplest suitable tool.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy
import sklearn
import statsmodels

print('NumPy:', np.__version__)
print('pandas:', pd.__version__)
print('SciPy:', scipy.__version__)
print('scikit-learn:', sklearn.__version__)
print('statsmodels:', statsmodels.__version__)
# NumPy: arrays; pandas: labelled tables; Matplotlib: figures;
# SciPy: scientific algorithms; sklearn: prediction; statsmodels: inference.
Expected output / interpretation
The cell runs without hidden variables from another example.
Run after: Requires the listed libraries in the active environment; versions are printed.
If it fails: Run the complete cell from the beginning. Confirm the package is installed in the active notebook kernel.
Import conventions used throughout scientific PythonNOTEBOOK CELL
The book uses short conventional aliases. Consistent imports make examples easier to read, but avoid importing everything with a wildcard because it hides where functions come from.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as st
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

print(np.__name__, pd.__name__, plt.__name__, st.__name__, sm.__name__, smf.__name__)
Expected output / interpretation
The conventional aliases are printed.
Run after: Run once near the top of a notebook; later examples may repeat imports when they need to be independently runnable.
If it fails: Run the complete cell. Check that the required package is installed in the active kernel.
Python as a data-analysis toolkitNOTEBOOK CELL
Python acts as a common environment that connects data structures, numerical arrays, statistics, models and visualisation. A single analysis can use each library for the task it handles best.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

measurements = pd.DataFrame({'group':['A','A','B','B'], 'hb_gdl':[10.1,10.8,11.4,12.0]})
array = measurements['hb_gdl'].to_numpy()
print('pandas mean by group:')
print(measurements.groupby('group')['hb_gdl'].mean())
print('NumPy mean:', round(np.mean(array), 2))
print('SciPy one-sample test against 11:', stats.ttest_1samp(array, popmean=11))
Expected output / interpretation
The cell runs without hidden variables from another example.
Run after: Pandas groups the data, NumPy calculates an array summary and SciPy performs a statistical test. The test is illustrative, not a research conclusion.
If it fails: Run the complete cell. Check that the required package is installed in the active kernel.

Book orientation: use official documentation and release notes when package behaviour changes; community forums and scientific Python conferences are useful for learning, but verify answers against documentation. The book’s data files and import conventions are part of reproducibility: record versions, keep source data unchanged and state which examples use simulated data.

Chapter 2: Python language basics and fundamentals

Here you learn the basic language used to give instructions to a computer: values, variables, text, numbers, lists, dictionaries, conditions, loops and functions. These are the building blocks you will use later to organise participant records and automate repetitive research tasks.

Variables, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions and error handling, illustrated with clinical values.

Book alignment: Python for Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Chapter 2 — interpreter basics, IPython/Jupyter workflow, notebook cells, introspection, Python syntax, objects, scalar types and control flow. The examples below adapt these ideas to simulated Biomedical research scenarios; they are original teaching examples, not copied book exercises.

Teaching and advanced learning clues
  • Use patient-style examples, never abstract foo and bar.
  • Let learners break the code on purpose and read the error.
  • Pair tasks: one writes, one reviews.
  • Write a function with type hints and a docstring.
  • Refactor a loop into a list comprehension and compare readability.
  • Add a unit check with assert.

Ex: write a function classifying birth weight (<2500 g LBW). Q: when use a dictionary instead of a list?

Your first Python calculation: gestational ageNOTEBOOK CELL
A notebook cell runs Python statements and displays the final expression automatically. Start with simple numeric calculations before working with a dataset. Dependencies: None; run in a Python notebook cell, not Command Prompt.
gestational_age_weeks = 32
additional_days = 4

total_days = gestational_age_weeks * 7 + additional_days
print(total_days)
print(f"Gestational age: {gestational_age_weeks}+{additional_days} weeks")
Expected output / behaviour
228
Gestational age: 32+4 weeks
Run after: Independent example; no earlier chapter data required.

Boolean logic: classify a measurement carefullyNOTEBOOK CELL
Comparison operators produce True or False. Missing values need separate handling; do not silently classify an unknown result as normal. Dependencies: None; run in a Python notebook cell, not Command Prompt.

elif hb_g_dl < 11:

else:

for loops: repeat a calculation across observationsNOTEBOOK CELL
A loop repeats the same operation for each item. This is useful for learning, although pandas will usually be preferable for operations on full columns later. Dependencies: None; run in a Python notebook cell, not Command Prompt.

for index, hb in enumerate(hb_values, start=1):

Assertions: check assumptions before analysisNOTEBOOK CELL
Assertions are simple checks for expected conditions. They do not replace a full data-quality plan, but they can catch mistakes early. Dependencies: None; run in a Python notebook cell, not Command Prompt.
birth_weights_g = [2860, 2410, 3150, 1980, 3020]

assert len(birth_weights_g) == 5
assert all(weight > 0 for weight in birth_weights_g)
assert all(isinstance(weight, (int, float)) for weight in birth_weights_g)

print("Basic checks passed")
Expected output / behaviour

Chapter 3: Built-in data structures, functions and files

This chapter teaches the everyday containers Python uses to organise research information, how to write reusable functions, how to handle errors, and how to read and write files safely. These skills help you build analysis workflows that are clear, repeatable and easier to check.

Book alignment: tuples, lists, dictionaries, sets, sequence functions, comprehensions, functions and scope, return values, lambdas, generators, exceptions, file handling, encodings and operating-system paths are taught here. The additional biomedical examples are teaching adaptations.

Functions: reuse a validated calculationNOTEBOOK CELL
A function packages a calculation. A docstring explains its purpose; input checks prevent invalid values from producing misleading results. Dependencies: None; run in a Python notebook cell, not Command Prompt.
def calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_m):
    """Calculate BMI from weight in kg and height in metres."""
    if height_m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Height must be greater than zero metres.")
    if weight_kg <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Weight must be greater than zero kilograms.")
    return round(weight_kg / height_m ** 2, 1)

print(calculate_bmi(68, 1.62))

Function scope and returning multiple valuesNOTEBOOK CELL
Local variables inside a function do not overwrite variables outside it. Returning multiple values makes a calculation reusable and testable.
threshold = 11.0
def summarise_hb(values, cut_off):
    observed = [x for x in values if x is not None]
    mean_value = sum(observed) / len(observed)
    below_cutoff = sum(x < cut_off for x in observed)
    return len(observed), mean_value, below_cutoff

n, mean_hb, below = summarise_hb([9.8, None, 11.4, 10.2], threshold)
print(n, round(mean_hb, 2), below)
print('Outer threshold remains:', threshold)

Lambda functions for simple mappingsNOTEBOOK CELL
A lambda is a small anonymous function. Use it for short transformations; use def for reusable or complex logic.

get_hb = lambda record: record['hb']

def hb_category(value):
    return 'below 11 g/dL' if value < 11 else '11 g/dL or above'
print([hb_category(get_hb(row)) for row in records])

Generators for memory-efficient processingNOTEBOOK CELL
A generator yields one item at a time instead of building a complete list in memory. This is useful for large files or streams.
def positive_results(lines):
    for line in lines:
        if line.strip().lower() == 'positive':
            yield line.strip()

results = ['Positive', 'Negative', 'Positive', 'Unknown']
positive_only = positive_results(results)
print(list(positive_only))

Handle errors without hiding data problemsNOTEBOOK CELL
Catch only errors you can handle. Do not replace failed measurements with zero or silently discard malformed records.
values = ['10.2', '11.5', 'not recorded', '9.8']
parsed = []
invalid = []
for row_number, value in enumerate(values, start=1):
    try:
        parsed.append(float(value))
    except ValueError:
        invalid.append((row_number, value))
print('Valid values:', parsed)
print('Needs source review:', invalid)

Read and write text files with a context managerNOTEBOOK CELL
Use with open(...) so the file closes automatically. Specify an encoding to avoid platform-dependent text decoding.
from pathlib import Path

work = Path('chapter3_demo')
work.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
file_path = work / 'specimen_notes.txt'
with file_path.open('w', encoding='utf-8') as handle:
    handle.write('Blood culture\nUrine culture\n')
with file_path.open('r', encoding='utf-8') as handle:
    lines = [line.rstrip('\n') for line in handle]
print(lines)
Expected output / interpretation

Paths, bytes and Unicode textNOTEBOOK CELL
Pathlib handles file paths across operating systems. Text should be decoded with a known encoding; bytes are not the same as characters.

print('Character count:', len(decoded))
print(decoded)
print('Path example:', Path('data') / 'laboratory.csv')

Chapter 4: NumPy basics — arrays and vectorised computation

NumPy is a Python library for working efficiently with numerical data. It stores values in arrays and lets you calculate across many measurements at once instead of writing a separate instruction for every participant. This is especially useful for laboratory concentrations, birth measurements and simulated datasets.

NumPy provides efficient numerical arrays. Learn array creation, shape, indexing, vectorised calculations, Boolean masks and missing-value-aware summaries before moving to pandas.

Book alignment: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (2022). Biomedical examples are adapted teaching scenarios with simulated data; they are not copied from the book.

NumPy: vectorised Biomedical calculations

Convert birth weights and calculate summariesNOTEBOOK
NumPy applies the conversion to every value at once. ddof=1 calculates the sample standard deviation.
import numpy as np
birth_weight_g = np.array([2860, 3120, 2450, 2980, 3350])
birth_weight_kg = birth_weight_g / 1000
print(birth_weight_kg)
print("Mean (g):", birth_weight_g.mean())
print("SD (g):", birth_weight_g.std(ddof=1))

print(low_bw)

4.6 — Basic linear algebra: matrix multiplication and solveNOTEBOOK CELL
Book-aligned NumPy example with synthetic biomedical teaching data. The @ operator performs matrix multiplication. solve finds x in A x = b; this is a numerical linear algebra example, not automatically a regression model.
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 3.0]])
b = np.array([5.0, 6.0])
print("A @ b:", A @ b)
solution = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print("solution:", solution)
print("check:", A @ solution)

solution: [1.8 1.4]
check: [5. 6.]

4.7 — Simulate one random walkNOTEBOOK CELL
Book-aligned NumPy example with synthetic biomedical teaching data. A random walk is a simple stochastic process. This example illustrates cumulative sums and simulation, not disease transmission or patient prognosis.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
steps = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=12)
position = steps.cumsum()
print("steps:", steps)
print("positions:", position)
print("final position:", position[-1])

4.7 Example: random walks

4.7 — Simulate many random walks togetherNOTEBOOK CELL
Book-aligned NumPy example with synthetic biomedical teaching data. The matrix stores five walks in parallel; axis=0 accumulates time down rows. Vectorisation avoids writing a separate loop for each walk.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n_steps = 100
n_walks = 5
steps = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=(n_steps, n_walks))
paths = steps.cumsum(axis=0)
print("steps shape:", steps.shape)
print("paths shape:", paths.shape)
print("final positions:", paths[-1])
Expected output / interpretation
steps shape: (100, 5)
paths shape: (100, 5)
final positions: [values depend on the seeded simulation]

How Chapter 4 connects to biomedical data workflows

Use NumPy when data are primarily numerical arrays and you need efficient element-wise calculations, simulation, matrix operations or numerical summaries.

Use pandas when observations need row and column labels, mixed data types, dates, joins, grouped summaries and transparent handling of missing records. NumPy arrays and pandas objects work together, but they are not interchangeable in every situation.

Before analysis, verify units, dimensions, participant ordering, missing-value codes and the meaning of each axis. A numerically valid result can still be scientifically wrong if the data structure or measurement units are misunderstood.

The synthetic examples are for programming instruction only. Clinical thresholds, assay cut-offs, diagnostic accuracy definitions and statistical analysis plans must come from the study protocol and validated references.

Primary programming reference: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition, O’Reilly Media, 2022, Chapter 4 (pp. 83–121). Explanations and biomedical examples in this learning library are original teaching material; they are not reproduced from the book.

Chapter 5: Getting started with pandas

Pandas gives Python table-like structures called Series and DataFrames. You can select columns, filter participants, sort records, calculate summaries and align information by labels. Think of a DataFrame as a programmable research spreadsheet that can handle much larger and more repeatable workflows.

pandas introduces Series and DataFrames. Practise creating tables, selecting columns and rows, filtering observations, adding derived variables and summarising data. All values here are simulated.

Chapter 6: Data loading, storage and file formats

Research information arrives in many formats, including CSV, Excel, JSON and databases. This chapter shows how to load these files into Python, control how columns are interpreted, and save cleaned or summarised outputs. Choosing the correct file format and data types helps prevent errors during analysis.

Read CSV and Excel files, inspect file paths, select sheets, control data types and dates, and export analysis-ready data. Edit the example paths and sheet names to match your computer.

Book alignment: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (2022). Biomedical examples are adapted teaching scenarios with simulated data; they are not copied from the book.

Read a CSV using an explicit pathNOTEBOOK CELL
Reads a small local CSV. Replace file_path with your approved data path when using your own file; the example uses source_df so it does not overwrite the main Biomedical training dataset.
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

data_dir = Path('chapter6_demo')
data_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
file_path = data_dir / 'sample_data.csv'
if not file_path.exists():
    pd.DataFrame({'participant_id':['P001','P002','P003'], 'hb_gdl':[10.2,11.5,
        9.8]}).to_csv(file_path, index=False)
source_df = pd.read_csv(file_path)
print(source_df.head())
print(source_df.shape)

Chapter 6 expanded: reading, writing and exchanging research data

This expansion follows the book’s data-loading chapter: delimited text files, flexible parsing, dates and missing-value markers, chunked reading, JSON and XML, binary storage, web/API-style data exchange and database connections. Read a large CSV in manageable chunksNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas and NumPy unless otherwise stated. chunksize returns an iterator of smaller DataFrames. This is useful when a dataset is too large to load all at once.
import pandas as pd

file_path = "python_data_loading_demo/Biomedical_cohort.csv"
positive_count = 0
row_count = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(file_path, chunksize=2):
    positive_count += chunk["malaria_status"].eq("positive").sum()
    row_count += len(chunk)
print("Rows processed:", row_count)
print("Malaria-positive records:", positive_count)

Read and write JSON recordsNOTEBOOK CELL

C. Databases and data exchange

Write a small research table to SQLite and query itNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas and NumPy unless otherwise stated. SQLite is included with Python. SQL filters records inside the database before returning them to pandas.
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P02", "P03"], "hb": [10.2, 12.4, 9.8]})
connection = sqlite3.connect("python_data_loading_demo/research_demo.sqlite")
df.to_sql("participants", connection, if_exists="replace", index=False)
query = "SELECT participant_id, hb FROM participants WHERE hb < 11"
low_hb = pd.read_sql_query(query, connection)
print(low_hb)
connection.close()
Expected output / interpretation
P01 and P03 are returned because their simulated Hb values are below 11 g/dL.

Create a reproducible import auditNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas and NumPy unless otherwise stated. A simple audit records what was imported and basic structural checks. For real studies, also record date, source, version, software and transformation decisions.
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

path = Path("python_data_loading_demo/Biomedical_cohort.csv")
raw = pd.read_csv(path)
audit = {
    "file_name": path.name,
    "file_size_bytes": path.stat().st_size,
    "rows": raw.shape[0],
    "columns": raw.shape[1],
    "column_names": raw.columns.tolist(),
    "missing_cells": int(raw.isna().sum().sum())
}
for key, value in audit.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

Data-loading decision guide

Format / sourceTypical pandas functionImportant consideration
CSV / TSV / delimited textread_csv()Check delimiter, encoding, header, missing codes and data types.
Excel workbookread_excel() / ExcelFile()Inspect sheet names; preserve raw workbook and select the correct sheet.
JSONread_json() / json_normalize()Choose the correct orientation; nested records may need normalization.
XMLread_xml()Check element structure and XPath; nested XML may need additional parsing.
Pickleread_pickle()Python-specific; only load trusted files.
Parquetread_parquet()Efficient columnar storage; requires pyarrow or fastparquet.
SQL databaseread_sql_query() / to_sql()Use explicit queries and protect credentials and identifiers.

Research data protection: use de-identified or synthetic records in teaching notebooks. Do not upload identifiable participant data to public services. Keep a read-only raw-data copy, document import options, and verify row counts, variable names, units, date parsing and missingness immediately after import.

Create the simulated Biomedical training files (run once)NOTEBOOK CELL
Creates five small CSV/Excel teaching files for the later examples. Every record is synthetic. The cell does not overwrite files that already exist. Run it once before importing the files; use your own approved dataset for actual research.
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# All records created here are SIMULATED teaching data, not real participants.
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
DATA = Path.cwd() / "Biomedical_training_data"
DATA.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Dataset A: one row per simulated maternal-newborn participant.
n = 500
ids = [f"M{i:04d}" for i in range(1, n + 1)]
age = rng.integers(18, 41, n)
parity = rng.poisson(1.6, n).clip(0, 8)
bmi = rng.normal(25.0, 4.2, n)
gest = np.clip(rng.normal(38.0, 2.0, n), 28, 42)
malaria = rng.binomial(1, 0.28, n)
hb = 11.7 - 0.75 * malaria - 0.035 * (bmi - 25) + rng.normal(0, 1.15, n)
sbp = np.clip(rng.normal(112, 13, n) + 0.25 * age, 80, 190)
dbp = np.clip(rng.normal(72, 9, n), 45, 120)
bw = 3050 + 105 * (gest - 38) - 230 * malaria + 7 * (age - 27) + rng.normal(0, 390, n)
bw = np.clip(bw, 900, 4800).round(0)
apgar = np.clip(np.rint(rng.normal(8.2, 1.0, n) - 0.5 * malaria), 1, 10).astype(int)
A = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": ids, "maternal_age": age, "parity": parity,
    "bmi": bmi.round(1), "gest_age_wk": gest.round(1),
    "hb_gdl": hb.round(1), "sbp": sbp.round(0), "dbp": dbp.round(0),
    "placental_malaria": malaria, "birth_weight_g": bw,
    "apgar_5min": apgar, "preterm": (gest < 37).astype(int),
    "lbw": (bw < 2500).astype(int)
})
A.loc[rng.choice(n, 20, replace=False), "bmi"] = np.nan
A.loc[rng.choice(n, 25, replace=False), "hb_gdl"] = np.nan

# Dataset B: placental malaria and inflammatory/laboratory markers.
parasite_density = np.where(malaria == 1, rng.lognormal(5.2, 0.7, n), 0.0)
B = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": ids,
    "placental_malaria": malaria,
    "parasite_density": parasite_density.round(1),
    "IL6_pgml": np.maximum(0.2, 3.5 + 0.0018 * parasite_density + rng.lognormal(1.1,
        0.55, n)),
    "TNFa_pgml": np.maximum(0.1,
        2.0 + 0.0009 * parasite_density + rng.lognormal(0.8, 0.5, n))
})

# Dataset C: balanced repeated biomarker measurements at four visits.
n_rep = 120
rep_ids = [f"R{i:04d}" for i in range(1, n_rep + 1)]
subject_effect = rng.normal(0, 1.4, n_rep)
C_data = pd.DataFrame([
    {"id": pid, "visit": visit,
     "biomarker": round(8.0 + subject_effect[j] + 0.55 * (visit - 1) + rng.normal(0, 0.65), 2)}
    for j, pid in enumerate(rep_ids) for visit in [1, 2, 3, 4]
])

# Dataset D: simulated diagnostic marker and binary adverse outcome.
biomarker = rng.normal(1.0, 0.55, n)
prob_adverse = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-1.25 + 1.15 * biomarker)))
D = pd.DataFrame({"adverse_outcome": rng.binomial(1, prob_adverse),
    "biomarker": biomarker.round(3)})

# Dataset E: simulated time-to-event records for survival-analysis demonstrations.
E = pd.DataFrame({
    "time_days": np.maximum(1, rng.exponential(180, n)).round(0),
    "event": rng.binomial(1, 0.42 + 0.08 * malaria, n),
    "placental_malaria": malaria,
    "maternal_age": age,
    "hb_gdl": np.where(np.isnan(hb), np.nan, hb.round(1))
})

# Never overwrite existing training files or a user's own edited copies.
files = {
    "A_maternal_birth.csv": A,
    "C_repeated_measures.csv": C_data,
    "D_diagnostic.csv": D,
    "E_survival.csv": E,
}
for filename, frame in files.items():
    path = DATA / filename
    if not path.exists():
        frame.to_csv(path, index=False)
        print("Created:", path)
    else:
        print("Kept existing file:", path)
excel_path = DATA / "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx"
if not excel_path.exists():
    with pd.ExcelWriter(excel_path, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
        A.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="A_maternal_birth", index=False)
        B.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="B_placental_malaria", index=False)
    print("Created:", excel_path)
else:
    print("Kept existing file:", excel_path)

print("Training files are ready in:", DATA.resolve())
print("Reminder: these are simulated data; never report them as real study findings.")
Expected output / behaviour
Creates A_maternal_birth.csv, Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx (sheet B_placental_malaria), C_repeated_measures.csv, D_diagnostic.csv and E_survival.csv inside Biomedical_training_data. Existing files are left unchanged.

Chapter 7: Data cleaning and preparation

Data cleaning is the careful process of identifying missing values, duplicates, inconsistent labels, incorrect types and implausible measurements. Python can help detect these issues, but it cannot decide what the correct clinical value should be. Check questionable records against source documents and keep a record of every change.

Assess missingness, duplicates, inconsistent labels, data types and implausible values before analysis. Do not silently replace missing values or remove observations; document every decision.

Book alignment: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (2022). Biomedical examples are adapted teaching scenarios with simulated data; they are not copied from the book.

Chapter 7 expanded: practical data cleaning and preparation

This expanded laboratory follows the book’s data-cleaning workflow. Every code cell is self-contained and uses simulated biomedical data. Inspect flagged records against the source; do not delete, overwrite, or impute values automatically. Keep a raw copy and document each decision.

Build a complete missingness profileNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas; NumPy is required only where imported. Run the complete cell independently.
import pandas as pd

cohort = pd.DataFrame({
    "participant_id": ["M001", "M002", "M003", "M004", "M005"],
    "haemoglobin_g_dl": [10.2, None, 8.9, 12.1, None],
    "birth_weight_g": [2860, 2450, None, 3120, 2700],
    "placental_malaria": ["positive", "negative", None, "positive", "negative"]
})
profile = pd.DataFrame({
    "missing_n": cohort.isna().sum(),
    "missing_pct": (cohort.isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
    "observed_n": cohort.notna().sum()
})
print(profile)
Expected output / interpretation
A variable-level report shows the number and percentage missing, alongside observed counts. The participant ID should normally be complete; investigate missing IDs before linking records.

Create clinically meaningful groups with cutNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas; NumPy is required only where imported. Run the complete cell independently.
import pandas as pd

bw = pd.Series([1800, 2400, 2999, 3200, 4100], name="birth_weight_g")
bins = [0, 2500, 4000, float("inf")]
labels = ["low_birth_weight", "2500_to_3999_g", "4000_g_or_more"]
group = pd.cut(bw, bins=bins, labels=labels, right=False)
print(pd.DataFrame({"birth_weight_g": bw, "group": group}))
Expected output / interpretation
pd.cut applies prespecified thresholds. Here 2500 g is included in the middle category because right=False. Define cut-points from an accepted protocol or clinical definition, not from whichever split gives a preferred result.

Explore quantile-based groups with qcutNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas; NumPy is required only where imported. Run the complete cell independently.
import pandas as pd

hb = pd.Series([8.1, 9.0, 9.7, 10.2, 10.8, 11.4, 12.0, 13.1])
quartile = pd.qcut(hb, q=4, labels=["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"])
print(pd.DataFrame({"haemoglobin": hb, "quartile": quartile}))
print(quartile.value_counts().sort_index())
Expected output / interpretation
qcut creates groups based on ranks/quantiles, usually with similar numbers of observations. These sample-derived groups are useful for exploration but discard information and should not replace continuous-variable analysis without justification.

Flag potential outliers using the IQR ruleNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research teaching example. Dependencies: pandas; NumPy is required only where imported. Run the complete cell independently.
import pandas as pd

hb = pd.Series([8.2, 9.1, 9.8, 10.0, 10.3, 10.5, 10.8, 11.0, 11.2, 19.5],
    name="hb_g_dl")
q1, q3 = hb.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lower, upper = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
flagged = hb[(hb < lower) | (hb > upper)]
print("IQR bounds:", round(lower, 2), "to", round(upper, 2))
print("Flagged values:", flagged.tolist())
Expected output / interpretation
The IQR rule flags unusually distant observations for investigation. An outlier may be a valid extreme biological value, a unit error or a transcription error; do not delete it solely because it is flagged.

Supplementary Biomedical practice: data cleaning and quality assurance

Real datasets can contain missing values, duplicate records, impossible measurements and inconsistent entries. This chapter teaches you to look for these problems systematically, check them against the study protocol or source records, and document corrections instead of silently changing data.

Complete-case analysis can reduce precision and may be biased when inclusion depends on observed or unobserved data. Single mean/median imputation usually understates uncertainty and distorts relationships. Multiple imputation is one option when its imputation models are appropriate and a missing-at-random assumption is defensible conditional on included variables; it is not automatically preferred for every dataset. Include exposure, outcome, analysis variables and useful auxiliary predictors in the imputation model, respect variable types and bounds, inspect convergence, and compare with complete-case and plausible missing-not-at-random sensitivity analyses.

Teaching and advanced learning clues
  • Plant a known error in a copy of the data and have learners find it.
  • Compare complete-case and imputed results side by side.
  • Require a written cleaning log.
  • Visualise missingness patterns by group.
  • Test whether missingness depends on observed variables.
  • Compare MICE results across five imputations.

Chapter 8: Data wrangling — joining, combining and reshaping

Research projects often store participant details, clinical observations and laboratory results in separate tables. This chapter teaches you to join those tables using appropriate identifiers and reshape data between wide and long formats. Checking keys and row counts prevents accidental duplication or loss of participants.

Combine related tables only after checking keys and expected relationships. Reshape repeated-measure data between wide and long formats while preserving participant and visit identifiers.

Book alignment: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (2022). Biomedical examples are adapted teaching scenarios with simulated data; they are not copied from the book.

Joining, combining and reshaping

Worked examples use simulated values. Confirm your study definitions, units, coding and data structure before adapting them to research data.

Merge participant and laboratory tablesNOTEBOOK
A left join retains all participants and adds matching lab values. validate checks the assumed one-to-one relationship.
participants = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["M001", "M002", "M003"], "age": [22, 31,
    19]})
labs = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["M001", "M002", "M004"], "hb_gdl": [11.4, 9.8,
    10.2]})
merged = participants.merge(labs, on="participant_id", how="left",
    validate="one_to_one")
display(merged)
Run after: Run in a fresh cell. M003 has no lab result; M004 is not added.
If it fails: MergeError: check duplicate IDs. A many-to-one or one-to-many relationship needs a different validation rule.
Reshape repeated biomarkers from wide to longNOTEBOOK
Long format stores one participant-visit measurement per row and is often useful for longitudinal analysis.
wide = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["M001", "M002"], "TNF_T1": [12.1, 10.8],
    "TNF_T2": [14.0, 11.2], "TNF_T3": [13.4, 12.0]})
long = wide.melt(id_vars="participant_id", var_name="visit", value_name="TNF")
long["visit"] = long["visit"].str.replace("TNF_", "", regex=False)
display(long)

A MultiIndex stores participant and visit together as the row index. It is useful for repeated-measure data, but keep the identifiers available so rows remain traceable.

Compare inner, left, right and outer joinsNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

participants = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["P01", "P02", "P03"], "age": [22, 30, 27]})
labs = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["P01", "P02", "P04"], "hb_gdl": [10.4, 11.8, 9.9]})
for how in ["inner", "left", "right", "outer"]:
    result = participants.merge(labs, on="id", how=how, indicator=True)
    print(f"\n{how.upper()} JOIN ({len(result)} rows)")
    print(result.to_string(index=False))
Expected output / interpretation
INNER JOIN (2 rows)
 id  age  hb_gdl _merge
P01   22    10.4   both
P02   30    11.8   both

LEFT JOIN (3 rows)
 id  age  hb_gdl    _merge
P01   22    10.4      both
P02   30    11.8      both
P03   27     NaN left_only

RIGHT JOIN (3 rows)
 id  age  hb_gdl     _merge
P01 22.0    10.4       both
P02 30.0    11.8       both
P04  NaN     9.9 right_only

OUTER JOIN (4 rows)
 id  age  hb_gdl     _merge
P01 22.0    10.4       both
P02 30.0    11.8       both
P03 27.0     NaN  left_only
P04  NaN     9.9 right_only

Inner keeps matched IDs; left retains all participants; right retains all laboratory IDs; outer retains every ID. The indicator column shows where each row originated.

Merge using more than one keyNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

left = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P01", "P02"],
                     "visit": ["T1", "T2", "T1"], "hb_gdl": [10.1, 10.8, 11.2]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P01", "P02"],
                      "visit": ["T1", "T2", "T2"], "crp_mg_l": [8.0, 6.2, 9.1]})
merged = left.merge(right, on=["participant_id", "visit"], how="outer", indicator=True)
print(merged.to_string(index=False))
Expected output / interpretation
participant_id visit  hb_gdl  crp_mg_l     _merge
           P01    T1    10.1       8.0       both
           P01    T2    10.8       6.2       both
           P02    T1    11.2       NaN  left_only
           P02    T2     NaN       9.1 right_only

A participant can have several visits, so participant_id alone is not a unique key. Joining on both participant_id and visit prevents values from different visits being matched.

Validate a one-to-one merge and detect duplicate keysNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

participants = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["P01", "P02"], "age": [24, 29]})
lab_summary = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["P01", "P02"], "hb_gdl": [10.3, 11.5]})
valid = participants.merge(lab_summary, on="id", validate="one_to_one")
print(valid.to_string(index=False))

# This deliberately duplicated key violates the one-to-one assumption.
duplicated_labs = pd.concat([lab_summary, lab_summary.iloc[[0]]], ignore_index=True)
try:
    participants.merge(duplicated_labs, on="id", validate="one_to_one")
except pd.errors.MergeError as exc:
    print()
    print("Expected validation error:", exc)
Expected output / interpretation
id  age  hb_gdl
P01   24    10.3
P02   29    11.5

Expected validation error: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a one-to-one merge

validate checks the relationship you expect. A failed validation is a useful warning: inspect duplicated IDs instead of allowing an unintended row multiplication.

Understand many-to-many row multiplicationNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P01", "P02"],
                       "test": ["culture", "PCR", "culture"]})
alerts = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P01", "P02"],
                       "alert": ["review", "repeat", "review"]})
result = orders.merge(alerts, on="participant_id", how="inner")
print(result.to_string(index=False))
print("Rows before:", len(orders), "and", len(alerts), "| after:", len(result))
Expected output / interpretation
participant_id    test  alert
           P01 culture review
           P01 culture repeat
           P01     PCR review
           P01     PCR repeat
           P02 culture review
Rows before: 3 and 3 | after: 5

When a key occurs multiple times in both tables, pandas creates every matching combination for that key. This Cartesian multiplication may be correct, or it may reveal that the wrong key was chosen.

Keep overlapping variable names clear with suffixesNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

baseline = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["P01", "P02"], "weight_kg": [58, 70], "site": ["A",
    "B"]})
followup = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["P01", "P02"], "weight_kg": [60, 71], "site": ["A",
    "B"]})
combined = baseline.merge(followup, on="id", suffixes=("_baseline", "_followup"))
print(combined.to_string(index=False))
Expected output / interpretation
id  weight_kg_baseline site_baseline  weight_kg_followup site_followup
P01                  58             A                  60             A
P02                  70             B                  71             B

Suffixes preserve both measurements with explicit time-point labels. This is safer than accepting ambiguous weight_kg_x and weight_kg_y columns.

Use pivot_table when repeated key combinations need aggregationNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

replicates = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P01", "P01", "P02", "P02"],

                           "crp_mg_l": [8.0, 10.0, 6.0, 12.0, 9.0]})

participant_id           
P01              9.0  6.0
P02             12.0  9.0

pivot_table aggregates repeated combinations; here it calculates the mean of replicate measurements. Choose an aggregation rule based on the laboratory protocol, not convenience.

Convert wide repeated-measure data to long format with meltNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

wide = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P02"],
                     "il6_T1": [4.2, 5.1], "il6_T2": [3.8, 4.7], "il6_T3": [3.1, 4.0]})
long = wide.melt(id_vars="participant_id", var_name="visit_measure",
    value_name="il6_pg_ml")
long[["biomarker", "visit"]] = long["visit_measure"].str.split("_", expand=True)
print(long.drop(columns="visit_measure").to_string(index=False))
Expected output / interpretation
participant_id  il6_pg_ml biomarker visit
           P01        4.2       il6    T1
           P02        5.1       il6    T1
           P01        3.8       il6    T2
           P02        4.7       il6    T2
           P01        3.1       il6    T3
           P02        4.0       il6    T3

melt converts repeated-measure columns into rows. The participant identifier stays fixed, while visit and measurement values become variables suitable for grouping and plotting.

Reshape structured repeated data with wide_to_longNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

wide = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P02"],
                     "hb_T1": [10.1, 11.2], "hb_T2": [10.7, 11.6],
                     "crp_T1": [8.0, 12.0], "crp_T2": [6.0, 9.0]})
long = pd.wide_to_long(wide, stubnames=["hb", "crp"], i="participant_id", j="visit",
                       sep="_T", suffix=r"\d+").reset_index()
print(long.sort_values(["participant_id", "visit"]).to_string(index=False))
Expected output / interpretation
participant_id  visit   hb  crp
           P01      1 10.1  8.0
           P01      2 10.7  6.0
           P02      1 11.2 12.0
           P02      2 11.6  9.0

wide_to_long is useful when several variables share a consistent suffix pattern. The suffix identifies the visit; confirm that all columns follow the same naming convention.

Stack and unstack a hierarchical indexNOTEBOOK CELL
Simulated biomedical research example. Dependencies: pandas. This cell is self-contained and can be run independently.
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.2, 10.8, 11.4, 11.7],
              index=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["P01", "P02"], ["T1", "T2"]],
                                               names=["participant_id", "visit"]))
wide = s.unstack("visit")
back_to_long = wide.stack()
print("Wide form:")
print(wide)
print("\nBack to long form:")
print(back_to_long)
Expected output / interpretation
Wide form:
visit             T1    T2
participant_id            
P01             10.2  10.8
P02             11.4  11.7

Back to long form:
participant_id  visit
P01             T1       10.2
                T2       10.8
P02             T1       11.4
                T2       11.7
dtype: float64

unstack moves an index level into columns; stack moves columns back into an index level. Missing combinations may be introduced or omitted depending on the data and options.

import pandas as pd

measurements = pd.DataFrame({"participant_id": ["P01", "P01", "P02", "P02"],

T1       10.6      10.0

Grouping by an index level produces visit-level summaries across participants. This is descriptive aggregation; it does not account for within-participant correlation as an inferential repeated-measures model would.

Supplementary Biomedical practice: variable transformation

Data transformation means creating or rearranging variables so they answer a research question. Examples include calculating age groups, deriving anaemia categories from an appropriate definition, changing units and reshaping repeated measurements. Always preserve the original values and document how derived variables were created.

Create analysis variables and reshape.

Teaching and advanced learning clues
  • Have learners derive variables by code, never by hand.
  • Check every recode with a crosstab.
  • Draw the wide and long layouts on paper first.
  • Use pd.cut with right=False and explain the edge effect.
  • Reshape with melt and stack and compare.
  • Build a reusable derive function.
New variablesNOTEBOOK CELL
Categories and outcome flags. Dependencies: pandas. Common error: wrong file path, column name or package not installed in this kernel. Confirm clinical thresholds and population-specific definitions before analysis.
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

# Reload the named synthetic datasets for this example; do not rely on a stale df.
DATA = Path.cwd() / "Biomedical_training_data"
required_files = ["A_maternal_birth.csv", "C_repeated_measures.csv", "D_diagnostic.csv",
    "E_survival.csv", "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx"]
missing_files = [name for name in required_files if not (DATA / name).exists()]
if missing_files:
    message = f"Run Chapter 6 data setup first; missing files: {missing_files}"
    raise FileNotFoundError(message)
df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "A_maternal_birth.csv")
df["participant_id"] = df["id"]
df["malaria_group"] = df["placental_malaria"].map({0: "Negative", 1: "Positive"})
B = pd.read_excel(DATA / "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx",
    sheet_name="B_placental_malaria")
repeated_df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "C_repeated_measures.csv")
D = pd.read_csv(DATA / "D_diagnostic.csv")
E = pd.read_csv(DATA / "E_survival.csv")

df['bw_cat'] = pd.cut(df.birth_weight_g,[0,1500,2500,4000,9999],labels=['VLBW','LBW',
    'Normal','Macrosomia'])
# Nullable integer preserves missing Hb values instead of coding them as non-anaemia.
df['anaemia'] = df.hb_gdl.lt(11).astype('Int64')
df['htn'] = ((df.sbp>=140)|(df.dbp>=90)).astype('Int64')

Chapter 9: Plotting and visualisation

This chapter uses plotting tools to display distributions, comparisons, relationships and trends. You will learn how to make graphs that communicate the data honestly, with meaningful labels, units and legends. The examples use biomedical measurements, but the same plotting skills apply across research fields.

This chapter follows the book’s matplotlib plotting workflow: figures and axes, line plots, bar plots, histograms, scatterplots, annotations, legends, ticks, labels, subplots and saving figures. Biomedical examples use simulated maternal, neonatal, infectious-disease and laboratory data. Choose the display to match the variable type and research question; do not treat a graph as a statistical test.

Book alignment: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (2022). Biomedical examples are adapted teaching scenarios with simulated data; they are not copied from the book.

Plot haemoglobin by malaria groupNOTEBOOK
A boxplot compares the distribution of haemoglobin between malaria groups. This complete example creates its own simulated DataFrame, so it can run in a fresh notebook without relying on an earlier df variable. It does not establish statistical significance or causality.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Simulated teaching data: 20 participants, not real study observations.
data = {
    "participant_id": range(1, 21),
    "malaria_group": [
        "Positive", "Negative", "Positive", "Negative",
        "Positive", "Negative", "Positive", "Negative",
        "Positive", "Negative", "Positive", "Negative",
        "Positive", "Negative", "Positive", "Negative",
        "Positive", "Negative", "Positive", "Negative"
    ],
    "hb_gdl": [
        9.8, 12.1, 10.2, 12.5, 9.5,
        11.8, 10.5, 13.0, 9.2, 12.4,
        10.0, 11.9, 9.7, 12.8, 10.3,
        12.2, 9.4, 13.1, 10.1, 12.0
    ]
}
plot_df = pd.DataFrame(data)
display(plot_df.head())

plot_df.boxplot(column="hb_gdl", by="malaria_group")
plt.title("Haemoglobin by malaria group")

plt.xlabel("Malaria group")
plt.ylabel("Haemoglobin (g/dL)")

Add a fitted line to a scatterplotNOTEBOOK CELL
A fitted straight line summarises a linear trend. It does not establish causation; inspect residuals and model assumptions and report the estimated slope with uncertainty.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(31)
age = rng.uniform(18, 40, 70)
birth_weight = 2400 + 18 * age + rng.normal(0, 350, 70)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(age, birth_weight, 1)
x_line = np.linspace(age.min(), age.max(), 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(age, birth_weight, alpha=0.65, label="Participants")
ax.plot(x_line, intercept + slope*x_line, label="Fitted linear trend")
ax.set(title="Maternal age and birth weight", xlabel="Maternal age (years)",
    ylabel="Birth weight (g)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Illustrative slope: {slope:.1f} g per year")

Heatmap: visualise correlations among biomarkersNOTEBOOK CELL
A heatmap uses colour intensity to show values in a matrix. Correlations can reveal patterns among biomarkers, but correlated variables do not necessarily have a causal relationship.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(44)
data = rng.normal(size=(120, 4))
data[:, 1] = 0.65*data[:, 0] + 0.76*rng.normal(size=120)
data[:, 2] = -0.45*data[:, 0] + 0.89*rng.normal(size=120)
corr = np.corrcoef(data, rowvar=False)
labels = ["CRP", "IL-6", "TNF-alpha", "Hb"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
im = ax.imshow(corr, vmin=-1, vmax=1, cmap="coolwarm")
ax.set_xticks(range(4), labels, rotation=25)
ax.set_yticks(range(4), labels)
for i in range(4):
    for j in range(4): ax.text(j, i, f"{corr[i,j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Pearson correlation")
ax.set_title("Illustrative biomarker correlation matrix")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Choose a graph that matches the research questionNOTEBOOK CELL

Supplementary Biomedical practice: data visualisation

Visualisation turns rows of numbers into pictures that help reveal distributions, differences, patterns and unusual observations. This chapter teaches you to choose suitable graphs, label axes and units clearly, and avoid misleading displays. A graph helps you explore and explain data; it does not by itself prove a scientific claim.

Label axes with units; export at 300 dpi.

Teaching and advanced learning clues
  • Critique a poor figure together before building a good one.
  • Insist on units, legends and captions.
  • Test figures in grey-scale.
  • Build a multi-panel publication figure with shared axes.
  • Set a house style with rcParams.
  • Export vector PDF and 300 dpi PNG.

Kaplan-MeierNOTEBOOK CELL
Kaplan–Meier curves are estimated with statsmodels, which avoids requiring lifelines. The training survival file is created by the earlier simulated-data setup cell.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.duration.survfunc import SurvfuncRight

E = pd.read_csv(DATA / 'E_survival.csv')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for group, label in [(0, 'No placental malaria'), (1, 'Placental malaria')]:
    subset = E.loc[E['placental_malaria'].eq(group)]
    km = SurvfuncRight(subset['time_days'], subset['event'])
    ax.step(km.surv_times, km.surv_prob, where='post', label=label)
ax.set(xlabel='Days', ylabel='Event-free probability', ylim=(0, 1))
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Execution note: the displayed implementation uses statsmodels, not lifelines. The survival-method code was checked in the build environment with statsmodels 0.14.6 on synthetic data; run it after creating the named survival dataset.

Chapter 10: Data aggregation and group operations

Often you need to compare summaries across groups, such as mean haemoglobin by malaria status or culture positivity by specimen type. Group operations let you split data into categories, calculate summaries for each group and attach group-level results back to individual records.

Use groupby to describe subgroups, apply transformations at participant or group level, and keep denominators visible. Distinguish descriptive summaries from inferential comparisons.

Book alignment: Wes McKinney, Python for Data Analysis, 3rd edition (2022). Biomedical examples are adapted teaching scenarios with simulated data; they are not copied from the book.

    'birth_weight_g': [2450, 2700, 3100, 2950]})
summary = df.groupby('malaria')['birth_weight_g'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'std']).round(1)
print(summary)

Summarise characteristics by exposure groupNOTEBOOK
Named aggregation creates readable group summaries. Add denominators and missingness when reporting results.
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

# Reload the named synthetic datasets for this example; do not rely on a stale df.
DATA = Path.cwd() / "Biomedical_training_data"
required_files = ["A_maternal_birth.csv", "C_repeated_measures.csv", "D_diagnostic.csv",
    "E_survival.csv", "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx"]

df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "A_maternal_birth.csv")
df["participant_id"] = df["id"]
df["malaria_group"] = df["placental_malaria"].map({0: "Negative", 1: "Positive"})
B = pd.read_excel(DATA / "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx",
    sheet_name="B_placental_malaria")

summary = df.groupby("malaria_group").agg(
    n_participants=("participant_id", "nunique"),
    mean_age=("maternal_age", "mean"),
    sd_age=("maternal_age", "std"),
    mean_birth_weight=("birth_weight_g", "mean")
).round(1)

Report outcome availability by groupNOTEBOOK
Makes group-specific outcome missingness visible before complete-case analysis.
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

# Reload the named synthetic datasets for this example; do not rely on a stale df.
DATA = Path.cwd() / "Biomedical_training_data"
required_files = ["A_maternal_birth.csv", "C_repeated_measures.csv", "D_diagnostic.csv",
    "E_survival.csv", "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx"]
missing_files = [name for name in required_files if not (DATA / name).exists()]
if missing_files:
    message = f"Run Chapter 6 data setup first; missing files: {missing_files}"
    raise FileNotFoundError(message)
df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "A_maternal_birth.csv")
df["participant_id"] = df["id"]
df["malaria_group"] = df["placental_malaria"].map({0: "Negative", 1: "Positive"})
B = pd.read_excel(DATA / "Biomedical_simulated_datasets.xlsx",
    sheet_name="B_placental_malaria")
repeated_df = pd.read_csv(DATA / "C_repeated_measures.csv")
D = pd.read_csv(DATA / "D_diagnostic.csv")
E = pd.read_csv(DATA / "E_survival.csv")

availability = df.groupby("malaria_group")["birth_weight_g"].agg(observed="count",
    total="size")
availability["missing"] = availability["total"] - availability["observed"]
availability["missing_pct"] = (availability["missing"] / availability["total"] * 100).round(1)
display(availability)
